collection.credit:
NEW EVENTS — HISTORY AND COLLECTIVE MEMORY (HIS-01..50, draft for the owner, 2026-11-15)
Old stories, ruins and abandoned places, heirlooms, disputed records, festivals that changed, names on carvings, customs nobody can explain, and the things a people remembers together: some of it painful and handled gently, some of it gloriously silly.
Written in the style of the owner's own events. Edit anything and send it back; nothing ships until you approve.

ledger.why: the casting line, carried out as the roles' ages (picks an elder and a teen aged 14-17)

collection.description: A teen asks an elder for the grown-up version of the story of the Long Walk Inland: tell them, or ask them to wait.

setup.name: The setup
setup.text: (friend) has heard the story of the Long Walk Inland a hundred times: how the village once moved from the coast to the hills for a season, singing all the way. (friend.He/she) is sixteen now, and (friend.he/she) has noticed the parts that don't make sense. Why did they move? Why so quickly? Why do some elders go quiet when it's told? (friend.He/she) asks (subject) for the grown-up version.

o1.name: Outcome A
o1.text: (subject) looks at (friend.him/her) for a long time. Then (subject.he/she) tells it, carefully. The village didn't move for fun. Strangers came from the sea, and they weren't friendly, and some people didn't make the walk. The singing was real, though: it was to keep the children calm. (friend) doesn't say anything for a while. "Thank you for telling me," (friend.he/she) says at last. (subject) nods. "You're old enough to carry a bit of it."

o2.name: Outcome B
o2.text: (subject) says, gently, "Not yet. When you're older." (friend) is frustrated. It doesn't feel fair. But (subject) doesn't change (subject.his/her) mind. "It's not a secret," (subject.he/she) says. "It's just heavy. You'll get it when you're ready to carry it." (friend) grumbles. That night, though, (friend.he/she) listens to the children's version at the fire with new ears.
